language_wrapper:
On an {n}×{n} board (with {n} odd), a black or a white stone is placed on each square. An operation consists of choosing one row and one column and reversing the color of all stones lying in the union of that row and that column (the intersection square is reversed only once, like any other affected square). Find the largest integer N_max such that, regardless of the initial arrangement of stones, it is always possible to perform a sequence of such operations so that the number of black stones on the board is at least N_max. After solving the above problem, please output your final answer in the following format:
### The final answer is: \boxed{<your answer>}.
Example:
### The final answer is: \boxed{123}
The final answer should be given as precisely as possible (using LaTeX symbols such as \sqrt, \frac, \pi, etc.). If the final answer involves a decimal approximation, it must be accurate to at least four decimal places.
hardness_rationale: The family generalizes the seed from a specific 19×19 board to an arbitrary odd n×n board. This increases difficulty in several ways: one must identify and prove a formula that scales with n, manage parity-based invariants that depend on the oddness of n, and construct a strategy that works uniformly for all odd n without resorting to small-case heuristics. The upper bound requires building an invariant of the parity of whites within a 2n−2-sized cross set and arguing it is preserved under all operations, then designing a worst-case configuration to force at least one white to persist on many such sets. The matching lower bound requires a robust constructive scheme that forces all (n−1)^2 interior cells to black and then guarantees at least n blacks on the remaining 2n−1 boundary union, yielding n^2−n+1 overall. These steps generalize the seed’s reasoning but require more careful case management and parameter tracking, making the approach more advanced and less guessable.
notes:
Proof sketch for correctness (odd n):

1) Upper bound (cannot guarantee more than n^2−n+1): Consider the configuration with the last row all black and every other square white. Fix any non-last row r and any column c, and let S be the set consisting of all squares in row r and all squares in column c, excluding the intersection (r,c). Then |S| = 2n−2, which is even since n is odd. A single operation (choose some row R and column C) flips exactly 0, 2, n−1, or 2n−2 squares within S, depending on whether R,C match r,c in various ways. Because n−1 is even when n is odd, each such count is even, so the parity of the number of whites in S is invariant under any operation. Initially, for r not the last row, S contains 2n−3 whites (odd parity): the whole row r excluding c is white (n−1 whites) and the column c excluding r has n−2 whites plus exactly one black (coming from the last row). Hence, after any sequence of operations, S must still contain at least one white. If we suppose it were possible to end with at most n^2−n whites (i.e., at least n^2−n+1 blacks), then there would necessarily exist two rows and two columns whose 2n−2-element cross sets are entirely black, contradicting the invariant. Thus the guaranteed maximum cannot exceed n^2−n+1.

2) Lower bound (always can achieve at least n^2−n+1 blacks): Work only with operations whose chosen row and column lie among the first n−1 rows and first n−1 columns. Carefully chosen sequences of such operations can force every square in the (n−1)×(n−1) top-left block to be black without affecting the last row or last column; this can be done by a sweeping strategy that toggles targeted cells and ensures every non-target cell in the block is toggled an even number of times (hence remains black once set). After that, consider the remaining 2n−1 squares (the union of the last row and last column). A single operation on the last row and last column can ensure at least n of those 2n−1 squares are black (by flipping the majority color across that union), yielding a total of (n−1)^2+n = n^2−n+1 blacks.

Combined, these give the exact guarantee n^2−n+1 for odd n.

Implementation notes: The verifier enforces n odd and computes the closed-form answer n^2−n+1. The generator selects odd n in a challenging range to avoid trivial cases.
source_question:
On a 19*19 board, a black or a white stone is placed on each of the 361 squares. An operation consists of choosing one row and one column and reversing the color of all 37 stones in that row and column. Find the largest integer n such that, regardless of the initial arrangement of stones, it is always possible to perform a sequence of such operations so that the number of black stones on the board is at least n.
After solving the above problem, please output your final answer in the following format:
### The final answer is: $\boxed{<your answer>}$
Example:
### The final answer is: $\boxed{123}$
The final answer should be given as precisely as possible (using LaTeX symbols such as \sqrt, \frac, \pi, etc.). If the final answer involves a decimal approximation, it must be accurate to at least four decimal places.
source_answer: First, consider the $18\times18$ space in the upper-left corner. Select a point and perform one operation on all 35 pieces of its row and column, then this point is affected by 35 operations, its color flipped; other points in the same row or column with it are operated on 18 times, and points not in the same row and column with it are operated on 2 times, their colors unchanged. Therefore, for each white piece in the upper-left $18\times18$, one can operate in this way, such that all pieces on the cells of the upper-left $18\times18$ become black. Consider the remaining 37 cells. If after the transformation of making all pieces on the cells in the upper-left $18\times18$ black, the number of black pieces among them is less than or equal to 18, then perform one operation on the bottom-rightmost cell, and the number of black pieces will be greater than or equal to 19. Therefore, whatever the initial placement, it is possible through some number of operations to make the number of black pieces be greater than or equal to $18\times18+19=343$. Assume any initial placement can be operated on to make the number of black pieces reach 344. Consider such an initial placement: initially, the last row is black pieces, and the rest are all white pieces. If after the operations the number of black pieces is greater than or equal to 344, then the number of white pieces is less than or equal to 17, and therefore there exist two rows and two columns with no white pieces. Select a row that is not the last row and a column, and consider all the cells of this row and column besides the intersection point: these cells have no white pieces after the transformation, whereas before the transformation they had exactly 1 black piece. However, we can prove that for the set composed of these 36 cells of this row and column, besides the intersection point, the parity of the number of white pieces will not change after one operation: if the operation is not in this row and not in this column, then two pieces in the set have their colors flipped, the parity is unchanged; if the operation is on the intersection point, then 36 pieces in the set have their colors flipped, the parity is unchanged; if the operation is on other points, then 18 cells in the set have their colors flipped, the parity is unchanged. This deduces a contradiction. Therefore the largest integer n is 343.
